analysis.one_liner: Narrows federal Clean Water Act protections to fewer waters and pays landowners double for lost property value.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply narrow which streams, wetlands, and other waters the federal government can protect under the Clean Water Act. It would strip existing agency rules and guidance defining those waters, bar agencies from writing new definitions without Congress, require written consent before federal inspectors enter private land, and force agencies to pay landowners twice the appraised loss when a water rule lowers property value — and the rule could not take effect until every landowner was paid.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and the industries that fill, drain, or discharge into small streams and isolated wetlands — developers, agricultural operations, and mining or energy projects — would face fewer federal permits, lower compliance costs, and double taxpayer-funded compensation when water rules cut into property value.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'navigable waters' to exclude wetlands without a continuous surface connection to protected waters, intermittently flowing channels, and storm-drainage structures, and bars regulators from 'aggregating' such waters to claim jurisdiction [S2][S3].
Declares groundwater to be state water and bans EPA from using the 'significant nexus' test to claim jurisdiction over waters [S2][S3].
Wipes out existing Corps and EPA rules and guidance defining protected waters, and forbids the agencies from issuing any new definition unless Congress expressly authorizes it [S3].

Requires federal agencies to pay landowners twice the appraised loss when a water rule diminishes property value or economic viability, and the rule has no force until all such claims are paid from the agency's own operating budget [S3].
Bars federal inspectors from entering private property to collect water data without the owner's written consent [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: fewer waters protected means more pollution and fill reaching the rivers, lakes, and drinking-water sources downstream, and taxpayers fund the doubled compensation payments through agency budgets.

drawbacks.text: Removing federal protection from most intermittent streams and non-adjacent wetlands would leave pollution and wetland destruction upstream unregulated, degrading the water that flows to everyone else [S2][S3].

The double-compensation rule, paid from agency operating budgets and suspending any new rule until all landowners are paid, would make federal water protections effectively unenforceable, since no agency could absorb open-ended liability [S3].

A fair objection supporters raise: after the Supreme Court's Rapanos decision, federal jurisdiction over isolated waters was genuinely unclear, and federal agents could enter private land to gather data without the owner's consent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a few legitimate property-rights fixes — clearer jurisdiction, consent for land entry — with sweeping changes whose main effect is stripping federal protection from most small streams and wetlands and making water rules financially impossible to issue. The protections removed cover the waters that feed drinking supplies and downstream communities, so the public cost plainly outweighs the narrow benefits, and the benefits flow mainly to those who develop, drain, or discharge into those waters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to two subcommittees, and sat there with no markup or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Rooney introduced the bill on March 29, 2012, joined by Reps. Glenn Thompson and Raul Labrador as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
Five Republicans cosponsored in total; no Democrat signed on [S4].

The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation and Water Resources and Environment subcommittees; no further action was ever taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal water regulators kept their existing authority, and the streams and wetlands the bill would have stripped from protection stayed under the Clean Water Act. Developers and extractive industries did not get the permitting relief or double compensation the bill promised.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Excluding intermittent streams and isolated wetlands from federal jurisdiction removes permitting hurdles and wetland-protection costs on land they want to build on; the pollution and flood-control value of those wetlands is lost by the communities downstream.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and pipeline operators
industries.note: Fewer waters under federal jurisdiction means cheaper disposal of fill and discharges from extraction and pipeline projects, with the environmental cost shifted to the public's water.
Declaring groundwater state water and exempting drainage channels and non-adjacent wetlands eases farm drainage and expansion, while runoff that reaches protected waters goes less scrutinized.
The bill pays them twice the appraised loss from any federal water rule that lowers property value, with taxpayers and agency budgets covering the bill and new rules frozen until all claims are paid.

industries.industry: Environmental regulators (EPA and Army Corps of Engineers)
industries.note: Existing jurisdiction rules would be voided, new definitions barred without Congress, and the agencies would carry unlimited double-compensation liability from their own budgets, hollowing out their ability to enforce the Clean Water Act.
